title: Boss: the permissions auditor
summary: Fix a scan report with symbolic chmod, solve a Permission denied ticket and audit with find -perm.

steps.title: Security review
body: Before go-live, security reviews the app server's files. Three tickets on a real machine: fix a scan report with
symbolic `chmod`, solve a "Permission denied" that only one user gets, and run a repeatable audit with `find -perm`.

steps.title: Fix a scan report with symbolic chmod
prompt: The security scan of `~/site` came back red. Fix each finding with **symbolic** `chmod` (`u+x`, `go-w`, `o=`),
which changes only the bits you name and leaves the rest alone:
1. `bin/*.sh` cannot be run: add execute for the **owner and group** only.
2. `conf/*.conf` are writable by group and others: remove **write** for group and others, keep their read.
3. `uploads/` is `777`: others must lose **write**, keep read and enter.
4. `public/index.html`: others must be able to **read** it, nothing more.
hints: Symbolic mode is *who* (`u g o a`), *op* (`+ - =`), *what* (`r w x`). Several clauses join with commas: `chmod u+x,g+x`.
solution: cd ~/site && ls -l bin conf public && ls -ld uploads
steps.explain: Octal sets all nine bits at once, so `chmod 755` on the wrong file can quietly *add* permissions. Symbolic mode says exactly what you mean ("take write away from others") and is safe to run on many files with different modes.

steps.title: bob gets Permission denied
prompt: Ticket: *"bob cannot read `/srv/app/config.yml`. ana can. Please give bob the same access as ana: he joined the
`devs` team. Nobody outside `devs` may read it."*
Find out **why** first (`ls -l`, `ls -ld`, `id bob`, `sudo -u bob cat /srv/app/config.yml`), then fix it with
`sudo`. Do not make anything readable by others.

checks.name: bob is in devs
checks.fail: `bob` is not in the `devs` group yet. `sudo usermod -aG devs bob` (the `-a` matters: without it, his other groups are removed).

checks.name: bob can read the config
checks.fail: `bob` still cannot read it. Every folder on the path needs `x` for him too: look at `ls -ld /srv/app`.

checks.name: ana can still read it
checks.fail: `ana` lost access. Keep her able to read it.

checks.name: eve (not in devs) cannot
checks.fail: `eve` is not in `devs` but can read the file. Others must get nothing.

hints: `ls -l /srv/app/config.yml` is `root:devs 640`: fine for the group. But `ls -ld /srv/app` shows the folder as `ana:root 750`. To open a file you need `x` on **every** folder on the way.
Two fixes: put bob in the group (`sudo usermod -aG devs bob`) and give the folder to that group (`sudo chgrp devs /srv/app`).
Test as him: `sudo -u bob cat /srv/app/config.yml`. A new group only counts in new logins, which `sudo -u` is.
explain: The kernel checks one triple per object: owner if you own it, else group if you are in it, else other. And it checks
**every directory** on the path for `x`. Half of all "Permission denied, but the file looks fine" tickets are a
parent folder. `namei -l /srv/app/config.yml` prints the permissions of every step of the path in one go.

steps.title: Audit with find -perm, then fix
prompt: Before the review meeting, audit `~/srv` with `find` and write the findings, one path per line, as `find ~/srv ...` prints them:
1. `~/answers/world-writable.txt`: everything (files and folders) that **others can write**.
2. `~/answers/secrets.txt`: secret files that the group or others can access **at all**: names ending in `.key`
or `.pem`, files named `.env`, and anything inside a `.ssh` folder.
Then fix them: nothing under `~/srv` may be writable by others, and the secrets must be owner-only (`600`).

checks.name: world-writable.txt is complete
checks.fail: The list does not match. `find ~/srv -perm -o+w` lists everything with the others-write bit (`-perm -MODE` means *all of these bits are set*).

checks.name: secrets.txt is complete
checks.fail: The list does not match. Group the name tests with `\( ... -o ... \)` and add `-perm /077` (*any* of the group or other bits).

checks.name: nothing is world-writable now
checks.fail: Something under `~/srv` is still writable by others.

checks.name: the secrets are 600
checks.fail: A secret file is not `600` yet.

hints: `find ~/srv -perm -o+w > ~/answers/world-writable.txt`. `-perm -o+w` means "at least these bits"; `-perm /077` means "any of these bits".
`find ~/srv \( -name '*.key' -o -name '*.pem' -o -name .env -o -path '*/.ssh/*' \) -perm /077 > ~/answers/secrets.txt`. Without the parentheses, `-perm` only binds to the last `-o`.
Fix with the lists you just made: `xargs chmod o-w < ~/answers/world-writable.txt` and `xargs chmod 600 < ~/answers/secrets.txt`.
steps.explain: An audit you can rerun beats one you did by eye: the same `find` commands go into a cron job or a CI check, and an empty result is the pass. `-perm -BITS` (all of them) and `-perm /BITS` (any of them) are the two forms to know.
